generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, so much learning happens through doing: running a study, presenting findings, a placement in a clinical or research setting. Left to itself, reflection on that work tends to stall at 'the session was hard'. A cycle such as Experience, Reflect, Act gives it a shape, so a seminar that fell flat or a data-collection session that overran becomes something you deliberately learn from, rather than simply move past.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students write a short reflection after the same group presentation on a research paper.

Tom writes that the presentation was stressful and the group ran over time, and resolves to be better prepared next time. This touches an experience, but it does not work through it: there is no real reflection on why it ran over, and the action, be better prepared, is too vague to act on. Tom has stopped at the experience and jumped to a resolution.

Amara starts from the same experience, then reflects: the group ran over because no one had agreed how long to spend on the methods critique, and the nerves came from not having rehearsed the handovers. From that, Amara settles on a concrete action, to propose a timed run-through at the next meeting and agree who speaks when. Experience, reflect, act: each stage done in turn.

Both wrote a reflection. Only Amara worked through the cycle, so only Amara came away with something usable.
generatedProse.summary: Structured reflection means working through an experience in set stages rather than at random, and a cycle such as Experience, Reflect, Act gives you those stages. You can now explain why a structure matters, recognise the stages at work in a psychology example, and apply the cycle to one of your own experiences. The next lesson works on the stage that does the most work: reflecting, rather than only describing.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection a worked-through cycle rather than a stalled one?

items.text: She reflected on why the presentation ran over, then set a concrete action from it.
She wrote more about the presentation than Tom did.
She resolved to be better prepared next time.
She found the presentation less stressful than Tom did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Reflecting on why it happened and then setting a concrete action is the cycle worked through.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara reflected on AND acted on, beyond the experience itself.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara worked through the cycle by reflecting on why it ran over and setting a concrete action. Writing more, resolving vaguely or feeling calmer are not the same.
